Question: What are the key findings from the differential geometry of curves?
Answer: I'm not aware what the OP wants to know from this question. Differential geometry of curves involves the Frenet frame attached to the curve. The frame constitutes T , N , B which are orthogonal vectors attached to the curve in space and form equations called the Frenet formulas which allow us to derive mathematical measurements of the turning and twisting of a curve in say R 3 . Later on, this Frenet apparatus was generalized by Darboux to the theory of surfaces by introducing the method of moving frames. Cartan brought this moving frame method to full generality. The essential idea is simple. To each point of the object under study ( a curve, a surface, a Euclidean space itself,..) assign a frame. Then using orthonormal expansion express the rate of change of the frame in terms of the frame itself. This, of course, is just what the Frenet apparatus does in the case of a curve. The choice of the frame is very important. Later on, when connection forms come into picture, the subject gets more generalized and sophisticated. Ordinary derivative is replaced with covariant derivative. What a connection one-form tells us? Take a look at the equation. ω i j ( v ) = ∇ v E i . E j ( p ) The connection one-form ω i j is the initial rate at which E i rotates towards E j as p moves in the v direction. Connection forms form connection equations. These equations have a striking similarity to the Frenet formulas for curves. All books on differential geometry which go upto connection forms display this obvious relation between the geometry of curves and geometry of surfaces. Remember, covariant derivatives treat curved surfaces and hypersurfaces. Finally, the connection forms satisfy the famous Cartan structural equations. Everything comes under the domain of differential forms. One equation connects dual forms to connection forms. Dual forms describe the dual of the frame field. Other equation connects curvature forms to connection forms. This looks complicated and boring. But this forms the basis of the calculation of curvature of spacetime in general relativity for several types of metrics. Misner-Thorne-Wheeler's Gravitation leans heavily on connection forms and curvature forms via Cartan's equations. And all graduate level texts such as Wald's General Relativity discuss curvature in terms of connection forms besides other methods. Eventually, the approach goes to the level of Newman-Penrose null tetrad method which is something of a “dinosaur” in calculating curvature of “unfamiliar" metrics of spacetime. What starts as a simple differential geometry of a curve in space gives rise to a very heavy mathematical technology in sophisticated forms of general relativity and other related topics in theoretical physics.

Question: What is the process for calculating the probability of finding electrons in a specific region using Schrodinger's wave equation?
Answer: This is a fine question. Ask for a potential V ( x , t ) in which your particle moves. Assume it is independent of time t . So, it becomes V ( x ) .Take your starting wavefunction Ψ ( x , 0 ) . Our job is to get the wavefunction Ψ ( x , t ) for any subsequent time t . To achieve this, we solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. You get, in general, an infinite set of solutions ( ψ 1 ( x ) , ψ 2 ( x ) , ψ 3 ( x ) . . . . ) . Each has its own energy, say, E 1 , E 2 , E 3 , . . Now to express Ψ ( x , 0 ) we consider the general linear combination of these solutions which equals our Ψ ( x , 0 ) . Ψ ( x , 0 ) = ∑ n = ∞ n = 1 c n ψ n ( x ) . Why we do this? Because, we can match the initial state by the correct choice of the constants c 1 , c 2 , c 3 , . . . Now you want the wavefunction Ψ ( x , t ) at a later time t . You just tack onto each term its characteristic time dependence e x p ( − i E n t / ℏ ) . The separable solutions are, Ψ n ( x , t ) = ψ n ( x ) e − i E n t / ℏ Calculate | Ψ | 2 . I have omitted many details such as the method of solving the Schrödinger equation, stationary states, probabilities and expectation values independent of time, etc. Consult the following relatively unknown Schaum book for introductory quantum mechanics. Good luck.

Question: Why aren't we taught the ‘Teichmüller theory' in undergraduate and graduate courses in mathematics? Is it only a PhD topic?
Answer: No. Teichmüller theory is taught at graduate level (US universities) and also at undergraduate. This is a beautiful theory which has ramifications well into every branch of mathematics. The following book is a great introduction to Teichmüller spaces which underlie the Teichmüller theory. This book is recommended by John Baez who is a mathematical physicist working in LQG for the last 30 years or so. What is a Teichmüller space ? The above book starts with basic notions of Riemann surface, genus, Riemann sphere, moduli spaces and finally the protagonist Teichmüller space. Teichmüller space may be defined as the space of equivalence classes of complex structures on a fixed surface of genus g, where two complex structures are counted as the same if they are biholomorphically equivalent. I assume that most terms are familiar to math students. What is the relation between Teichmüller space and moduli space. Teichmüller space, roughly, is a more fine-grained notion of moduli space. In a different way we can say that Teichmüller space are collections of possible complex structures that you can put on a given surface. What is the Teichmüller space of a sphere? A sphere has no holes. It has genus 0. The Teichmüller space is just a point since there is only one complex structure on it, the Riemann sphere! Now this is just the tip of the iceberg. Teichmüller theory is intimidatingly vast and complex. No wonder that it is generally discussed at research level. It has connections with string theory as well. I don't mention about Mochizuki's version of Teichmüller theory. His piece of mathematics is known to just countable number of first-rate mathematicians of the world including Peter Scholze.

Question: How does the language of QFT translate vague concepts into precise mathematical formulations?
Answer: Language of QFT is not vague. It is abstract. If you understand the formalism of QFT carefully, you will find that there are several results which encapsulate a physical idea and translate into a precise mathematical expression. Of course, when I say physical idea it means an idea which cannot be imagined in a classical manner. Take the following expression: G μ ν = ∂ μ A ν − ∂ ν A μ − i g [ A μ , A ν ] . This G μ ν is the non-abelian gauge field. The A μ are the vector potentials in terms of which the gauge field is expressed. The above expression tells you, roughly, how the gauge field G transforms when it is propagated from one point to the other. It is also called as the connection by physicists, because it connects the components of a vector at one point with its components at a nearby point. Here, we have the internal space rather than the curved spacetime of general relativity, where this rotation takes place. I said non-abelian gauge field above. This gauge field behaves differently from the abelian U ( 1 ) gauge field which is our familiar electromagnetic field F μ ν = ∂ μ A ν − ∂ ν A μ . What is the difference between these two expressions? The first one is the non-abelian gauge field, the second one is abelian. Mathematically, it means that the symmetry group of the first field is non-abelian, the symmetry group of the second field is abelian. Take the first gauge field as QCD, the interaction of quarks. Looking carefully at the above equations, we see that the third term in the first expression is absent in the second expression for the electromagnetic field. What it physically means? The third term − i g [ A μ , A ν ] reflects an important fact: the quanta of non-abelian gauge fields also interact with each other besides interacting with the quark field! The third term represents this interaction. For the electromagnetic field, this is absent thereby telling us that photons do not interact with each other than “mediating” the Dirac field (matter field). In other words, the quantity in the square brackets represents the interaction dynamics of the gauge particles among themselves. This term is called the commutator term. This is not a vague language, but one needs a careful study to obtain a physical picture from mathematical formalism and vice-versa. Without careful interpretation, the expression gets unintelligible. QFT is full of thousands of long, complex mathematical expressions. Hope this helps!

This is done via moving a tangent plane along the curve and looking at the normal vector to the tangent plane as to how much it tilts as we move along the curve. This is also done with the help of the Gauss map. This works along the same lines. Gauss map is the map from surface S to sphere S 2 . We have a surface patch σ : U → R 3 in S . Remember, the direction of the tangent plane to this surface patch σ is measured by the rate of change of N per unit area. Here the green area R is the image of σ under this map. This sends p to n ( p ) of S 2 . We focus on region R ⊆ U on S . We watch the amount by which n ( p ) varies the part σ ( R ) of the sphere by the area of the part n ( R ) of the sphere. Thus, the rate of change of n per unit area is given by the ratio. A ( n ( R ) ) A ( σ R ) Now the theorem linking these ideas says that as the region R shrinks to a point, this ratio becomes the absolute value of the Gaussian curvature of S. At every point of the argument above, we consider a normal direction to the surface in question. Therefore, there is no non-normal direction considered in the definition.

Question: Is the Cayley-Hamilton theorem is used in quantum field theory? If so, how?

Zettili's influential book on Quantum Mechanics works out several problems using Cayley-Hamilton theorem obtaining eigenvalues for several quantum observables. Quantum field theory is the “extension” of quantum mechanics. Therefore, even though this theorem does not directly contribute to a result in quantum field theory, this is cornerstone in the mathematical equipment of quantum mechanics and, indirectly, of quantum field theory.

Question: What are some of the best research papers in physics which I should read as a beginner? Also, what papers should I read specially in the field of astrophysics?
Answer: Should beginners read research papers ? I find strange. I have skimmed several papers. One paper is by Richard Feynman on quantum electrodynamics. From my point of view, this is one of the best papers in theoretical physics. This is a beautiful paper requiring few prerequisites of quantum mechanics, in particular, the Hamiltonian formalism and propagator approach. Feynman's language is very clear and clean. He is patiently telling us how electrons move from one place to the another. The mathematics is simple! Believe me! This is a 21-page paper which I had read somewhere around 2005. Though I was not prepared then with sufficient machinery of quantum mechanics to grasp basic notions of quantum electrodynamics, I kept on coming back to this paper later after expanding my understanding of Feynman diagrams, propagators, Green functions, etc. The most beautiful part of the paper is that Feynman interprets each Feynman integral in physical terms! He interprets each term in the most intuitive manner. This paper is charming in the sense that it does not stop you in-between. Feynman had a deep understanding of a subject as much as the way it should be described in the most elegant manner. Students of quantum mechanics should give some attention to this paper to appreciate QED as perceived by Feynman. The paper just opposite to Feynman's is Schwinger's paper: daunting and intimidating to even experts!

Question: Do all textbooks on quantum field theory start with classical mechanics?
Answer: Books on quantum field theory generally start not with classical mechanics but with classical field theory for “obvious” reasons . This is not a very big difference as such. However, this is not a strict trend either. Some authors (Ryder, Weinberg, Das) start the subject directly with relativistic quantum mechanics and some historical introduction without going into the classical mechanics part. It all depends upon how much the author expects you to understand from his book and reflects his/her own style.

Question: It is considered that the discovery of the theory of quantum gravity is googolplex times more difficult than the discovery of the theory of general relativity. So would be googolplex Einsteins working together enough to develop such a theory?
Answer: We don't require so many Einsteins. Quantum gravity is a different problem altogether. There are already more than 25 theories of quantum gravity, all of which are incomplete and inconsistent. A complete and consistent theory of quantum gravity must reduce in appropriate limits to known and established theories and this looks formidable. Few years back when I started studying loop quantum gravity and came across the formula for area operator and the “quantization of area”, I convinced myself that half the battle was over! If area and volume are quantized in terms of ℏ , then we can achieve quantum geometry, then quantum metric and then quantum curvature, etc. But it was not so. The “infamous” Hamiltonian contraint put a dead end to the enterprise. In simple words, you drive a certain distance toward destination, covering more than halfway and then suddenly your car breaks down and nobody knows how to set it right again. Penrose got stuck up in a similar way. He needed the full Einstein equations to be solved in the twistor framework. Nobody knows how to solve the full set of Einstein equations without invoking symmetry. At some time there are conceptual difficulties, at other times there are technical issues. Some people take the perturbation approach, some take the non-perturbative approach bypassing renormalizability of quantum gravity. These are grave conceptual issues and require some Einstein-Bohr like debate in modern perspective. Finally, nature has given us a limited life span. It is not possible for any single person or even for a group to understand everything in any given approach to quantum gravity and to look for other ideas prevalent in rival theories! Nearly 100 years back it was possible to compare Schrödinger's approach with Heisenberg's approach to quantum mechanics and prove their equivalence. It was possible to compare Feynman's way of quantum electrodynamics and Schwinger's method towards it and prove their equivalence. Now in 80 years, theoretical physics has become formidably multidimensional: mathematically, physically, geometrically, philosophically, etc. May be quantum gravity is still not a 21st century theory, but a 22nd century theory!
